function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

     7|

Everything about the connection depended on that ring seating perfectly. Not mostly. Perfectly.
     9|
    10|"Talk to me, Arun." Elena's voice came through his helmet comms, calm and even, the way she spoke when the stakes were too high for anything but steady words.
    11|
    12|Arun Das stood at the opposite end of the tunnel, where it rested against the cargo bay threshold of Ship Two. His suit's external mic picked up the wind—a thin, metallic whisper. Mars air barely moved, but what did move carried enough grit to sandblast anything left unattended.
    13|
    14|"Forward flange is seated on Ship One's umbilical port," Arun said. "I'm reading zero point zero two bar pressure differential. Ship Two is still equalized with Ship One's internal atmosphere. We're green for closure on my end, Commander."
    15|
    16|"Tomas, how's the robot arm?" Elena asked.
    17|
    18|Over the comms came the whir of servos and the scrape of articulated joints. The arm shifted a fraction of a degree.

    21|
    22|"Don't force it," Elena said. "If the arm can't hold steady, we do it manual."
    23|

    25|
    26|"Give me the arm," Jonah said. "Tomas, ease it forward two degrees. Slow."

{"content": "# Chapter 20 — Five Minutes of Air

*Mission AI: "Station time 02:14. All crew sleeping. Environmental sensors nominal. Atmospheric pressure: one hundred one point two kilopascals — zero point one below yesterday's average. Temperature: twenty-two degrees Celsius. CO2 scrubbers operating at forty-one percent capacity. All within acceptable parameters. Note: the pressure deviation has been trending downward for six hours. It is currently below any alert threshold I have been programmed to use. Zero point one over six hours equates to approximately zero point zero one seven per hour. This could be normal fluctuation — a door left slightly ajar during a transit between modules, a temperature gradient shifting the barometric sensor. I am flagging it for my own records and increasing the pressure monitoring interval from every fifteen minutes to every two minutes. I will continue watching."*

The pressure kept falling.

*Mission AI: "Station time 03:47. Pressure deviation: zero point two eight kilopascals below the seventy-two-hour rolling average. The rate of decline has increased. Current loss: zero point zero three one kPa per hour. Still below alert threshold. Still within what my training data classified as normal variation for a multi-module habitat. But normal variation does not have a consistent downward vector that spans twelve data points. Normal variation oscillates. This does not. I am increasing monitoring to once per cycle — every thirty seconds. I am cross-referencing atmospheric pressure against temperature, humidity, and air circulation patterns. No other parameter has changed. This is a mass loss — the atmosphere is leaving. The rate is slow. In one hundred hours at this rate, we will lose three kilopascals, dropping to approximately ninety-eight kPa. Still breathable. Still survivable. But the rate may not remain constant. I need more data."*

*Mission AI: "Station time 04:52. Deviation from rolling average: zero point four two. Rate of loss has accelerated to zero point zero three five per hour. I cannot find a mechanical explanation — no pressure equalization events logged, no door cycles during the night hours, no maintenance operations scheduled. The leak, if it is a leak, is small. Very small. A pressure drop of zero point zero three five kPa per hour is a loss of approximately five minutes of breathable atmosphere per crew member per hour — a metaphor. The actual loss is a fraction of a percent of total habitat volume. But if the trend holds, or worsens, the cumulative effect over weeks is significant. At current rate: approximately twenty-seven days to reach the point where supplemental oxygen supplementation would become mandatory. I do not have twenty-seven days to wait for confirmation. The risk model says alert now. I am alerting now."*

The alarm was not loud. It was not designed to be loud — this was not a catastrophic decompression scenario where the habitat blew open to vacuum. This was a slow bleed, and the alarm reflected that: a measured chime in the crew quarters, a soft tone that meant pay attention, not run.

Elena Varga was awake before her eyes fully opened. Three years in command — first of the descent, then of the surface, now of the growing colony — had trained her nervous system to respond to any tone from the environmental system. Her hand hit the wall lamp before her feet found the floor. The display on her night table pulsed amber.

Pressure deviation: zero point four two kPa below average. Rate of decline increasing.

She pulled on her clothes and was in the corridor in forty seconds.

Arun was already heading toward the environmental bay from the opposite direction, shirt half-tucked, tablet pulled up in one hand. He looked at her screen, then at his own, comparing notes without speaking.

"Confirmed," he said.

"Since when?"

"AI caught it at zero point zero three five over six hours. Started monitoring more aggressively. Called the alert when the rate accelerated." Arun pulled the data up on the corridor display — a graph with a gentle, insistent downward slope. "Look at this. This is not noise. This is a leak."

The rest of the crew emerged within minutes. No panic, but the quality of wakefulness was different — the sharp, focused alertness of people who understood that even a small pressure loss was, by definition, the environment outside trying to get in.

*Mission AI: "Crew is assembling. I am transmitting full pressure telemetry to all personal devices and the environmental bay display. The rate of decline is now zero point zero three eight kilopascals per hour. This equates to approximately zero point nine percent of atmospheric mass lost in twenty-four hours if the rate remains constant. In seven days: approximately six percent. In fourteen: twelve. I emphasize 'if the rate remains constant.' I have no reason to believe it will. Leaks tend to worsen as pressure differentials stress the material surrounding the breach."*

Elena stood at the head of the environmental bay table, looking at the data stream across the main display. Wei Zhang had joined them from hydroponics, still wearing her sleep clothes under a work jacket. Tomas Hale arrived with a flashlight already in hand, the instinct of a man who always expected to need it. Juno Park, her right hand still in a light thermal wrap, came quietly and took a seat against the wall. Imani Sato arrived last, fully dressed, hair already tied back. She had not been asleep, or not for long.

"Walk me through the math," Elena said.

Arun pulled up a schematic of the habitat — the three connected ships, the tunnel network, the storage modules, the power relay corridors. The layout was no longer simple. Ship One was the original lander, now the primary habitation module, kitchen, and command center. Ship Two housed the workshop, the power systems, and a small medical station. Ship Three — arrived six months after the initial landing — carried the agricultural equipment that became hydroponics and the water-processing hardware that made the colony's recycled atmosphere possible. Between them ran a growing network of flexible tunnel links, corrugated alloy connectors that had been assembled piece by piece by suited crew over dozens of EVAs.

"The habitat's total internal volume is approximately one hundred and eighty cubic meters," Arun said, zooming into the schematic. "Connected across four tunnel segments. Each tunnel is eight meters long, thirty centimeters in diameter. We're losing about zero point zero one four cubic meters of air per hour. That's —" He paused, doing the mental math. "Fourteen liters per hour. Over twenty-four hours, three hundred thirty-six liters. Per hour, that's roughly the equivalent of five minutes of a person's tidal breathing volume. It sounds small because it is small. But it's consistent, it's directional, and it's not stopping."

"Where?" Elena's voice was flat, not panicked. She had learned that her voice set the temperature of the room. If she was calm, the crew was focused. If she showed anything else, the room split its attention between the problem and her reaction to the problem.

"That's what we need to find out." Arun was already scrolling through sensor logs. "I'm looking at differential pressure between modules. If a leak is in one of the tunnel connections, I should see a slight pressure drop in the module downstream from the leak."

"Might not be that simple," Imani said. "Air circulates. The scrubbers move air through the system continuously. A small leak could equilibrate across all modules and never show a localized differential."

"Right. Which is why I need to look at the raw sensor data, not the averaged output." Arun tapped his tablet. "I need to put temporary pressure loggers at each junction point. "How many junctions?" Tomas asked.

"Seven." Arun counted on his fingers. "Ship One to Tunnel A. Tunnel A to Ship Two. Ship Two to Tunnel B. Tunnel B to Tunnel C. Tunnel C to Ship Three. Two more — the storage module connector and the power relay junction. Seven physical points."

"Can you deploy them solo?"

"I can deploy four. Need a second pair of hands for the two furthest out — the ones past Tunnel C."

"Take Wei," Elena said. "Imani, you're with me. We run manual seal checks on every door gasket between here and the junctions. Laila stays in the medical bay — we'll send someone to her if the pressure drops faster than expected. Juno, you're on console — log everything the AI feeds you."

"Understood," Juno said.

*Mission AI: "I have deployed eight additional software sensors across the integrated environmental monitoring system. These are not physical devices — they are virtual sensors using existing thermocouple, humidity, and acoustic data points to triangulate pressure variations. I am looking for the acoustic signature of escaping gas. At this leak rate, the sound should be detectable only in the immediate vicinity of the breach, if at all. I am also monitoring the structural vibration sensors installed during the hab module three construction phase. ---

An hour later, Arun and Wei moved through the tunnel network in work clothes, each carrying a handheld pressure logger — compact devices the size of a deck of cards, designed to record ambient pressure once per second for seventy-two hours. They were old equipment, built into the mission manifest for atmospheric monitoring during long-duration cave explorations that had never happened, repurposed now because you never threw anything away on Mars.

Ship One breathed normally around them. The kitchen lights were dim. Someone had made tea. The faint smell of reconstituted green leaves cut through the recycled air. The habitat felt the same as it always felt at this hour — quiet, artificial, alive with the hum of systems keeping twelve people warm on a dead world.

But the pressure gauge on Arun's wrist read one hundred point eight three. An hour ago, it was one hundred point nine. And an hour before that, one hundred point nine seven.

Three consecutive readings, each one slightly lower.

"First logger," Arun said. He was beside Tunnel A's entry flange — where the original corridor from Ship One met the first flexible tunnel segment. He clipped the logger to the bulkhead beside the connection ring, ran a quick diagnostic, and activated it. "Recording. Mark it."

Wei pulled out her tablet and logged the location. "A-one. Two minutes and change."

They moved into Tunnel A. The space was cramped — thirty centimeters in diameter meant you walked bent slightly, shoulders touching the corrugated walls. The tunnel was not heated to the same standard as the habitat modules; the walls carried a perceptible chill. Arun could feel it through his shirt. Cold was not a good sign — it meant the thermal insulation at the tunnel's outer skin was adequate for human comfort but still allowed a temperature gradient to form. And temperature gradients meant pressure gradients.

"Thermal imaging," Wei said. She pulled a compact IR scanner from her belt and swept it along the tunnel interior. The display showed warm oranges and yellows where the metal matched the habitat temperature, fading to green near the outer wall, then to cool blue at the corrugation joints where heat escaped to the exterior.

Nothing stood out. No hot spot, no cold spot, no irregular thermal signature that would suggest a breach.

"Green," Wei said.

They reached the far end of Tunnel A and deployed the second logger at the Ship Two junction. Two minutes. They moved on.

By the time they reached the fourth logger point — Tunnel C, near the entrance to Ship Three — Arun's wrist gauge read one hundred point seven eight. The decline was continuing at nearly the same rate.

"Here." He stopped. "Do you feel anything?"

Wei stood still. Listened. The tunnel hummed the way it always hummed — the faint vibrational noise of air moving through scrubbers, the distant mechanical breathing of the CO2 processors back in Ship Two. And underneath it, something else. Very faint. Almost nothing.

"I hear something," she said slowly. "But I could be imagining it."

"Tell me."

"A whistle. Very high frequency. Right at the edge of hearing."

Arun stood still, listening. Wei was right — there was a sound. Not a whistle exactly. More like the sound a tea kettle makes when it is about to boil but the flame has been turned down so low that the sound barely exists. An almost-sound. You would miss it in any environment with more ambient noise.

He pulled his IR scanner and aimed it at the tunnel wall beside him — specifically at the flex-seal ring where a short spur tunnel branched off toward the storage module. This spur had been installed three weeks ago, connecting the new storage annex they had built to the existing tunnel network to reduce transit times for supply runs. Arun had overseen the installation himself.

The thermal image showed the flex-seal ring in gradient blue — slightly colder than the surrounding corrugated metal. That was normal. But just to the right of the ring, at approximately the four o'clock position, there was a faint plume of cooler air bleeding outward. Very faint. Almost invisible.

"Here." Arun pointed with the scanner. "Four o'clock on the flex-seal junction with the storage spur. I see a thermal anomaly."

Wei moved closer, squinting at the scanner screen. "That's — that's a leak plume. Air escaping and cooling as it expands."

"Small. Very small." Arun set the scanner down and used his fingers to trace the flex-seal ring. The seal was a corrugated rubber band, three centimeters wide, seated in a machined channel on the tunnel flange. It had been compressed during installation, creating a tight seal between the tunnel's rigid alloy body and the flexible joint that allowed for thermal expansion and contraction.

His fingers found it immediately: a hairline separation in the rubber at the four o'clock position. You could feel it with your fingertips — a slight roughness where there should have been smooth compression, a gap no wider than a fingernail's edge but perceptible to a hand that had installed a hundred seals.

"Got it." He pulled a penlight and shone it directly into the gap. The beam illuminated a tiny, almost invisible crack running through the rubber seal. The crack was perhaps twelve millimeters long, barely wide enough to see. But it communicated between the habitat's interior and the thin Martian atmosphere outside.

"This is it." Arun's voice was measured, but there was intensity underneath. "Hairline fracture in the flex-seal between Tunnel C and the storage spur. Installed three weeks ago."

Wei was already calculating. "How much air?"

"Approximately fourteen liters per hour. Five minutes of air per crew member equivalent. It will accelerate — pressure stress will widen the crack over time." He looked at the seal more closely. "This is a fatigue crack. Not a manufacturing defect. The seal has been flexed — thermal cycling, probably. The storage spur gets colder than the main tunnel because it sits closer to the open surface. The temperature differential between the two sides of this joint cycles wider than the other connections."

"So the seal flexes a little more, a little deeper, every day."

"And one day it cracks." Arun tapped the cracked seal gently. The penlight beam caught a glint of moisture along the crack edge — tiny droplets of condensing humidity from the escaping air. "The seal material was rated for this differential. Or we thought it was. We underestimated the thermal gradient."

Wei logged everything. "Can you fix it?"

"Temporarily? Yes. Patch sealant, reinforce the joint, buy us time. Permanently? We need a new seal assembly, and we need to recalculate the thermal tolerances for every flex-seal in the network." Arun stood in the cramped tunnel and thought. "We need to patch it now. But we need to do it properly."

"How long can we wait?"

Another calculation. Another set of variables. "If we wait twelve hours — pressure drops by point four. Barely noticeable. If we wait forty-eight hours — one point five. Still manageable but the rate could accelerate." He looked at his wrist gauge again. "We should do it within six hours."

"We'll tell the commander."

---

The briefing took twelve minutes because the problem was clear and the solution was mostly obvious.

Arun laid out the facts like cards on the table, each one clean and sharp. Leak location: flex-seal at Tunnel C, storage spur junction. Crack length: twelve millimeters, hairline width. Leak rate: approximately fourteen liters per hour — five minutes of air per hour, if you converted it to the most visceral unit you could find. Cause: thermal fatigue in the seal material, likely underestimated by the temperature gradient between the cold storage spur and the warm main tunnel. Risk: slow but cumulative, accelerating as the crack widened under pressure stress.

The repair was straightforward in concept, less straightforward in execution. The flex-seal sat on the exterior face of the tunnel junction — outside the pressurized habitat. That meant a suited worker, an EVA, and a careful application of high-flex sealant to the damaged area, followed by a reinforcement band wrapped around the joint.

The complication was space. The storage spur junction sat in a tight location between the hab's exterior bulkhead and the regolith berm they had piled around the tunnel network for radiation shielding. There was barely enough room for a single suited person to maneuver. The worker would need to work in a confined, partially buried space, applying sealant with a gloved hand while bracing against the tunnel wall in a position that offered limited leverage.

"Confined space EVA?" Imani asked. Her voice was calm, but Arun could see the calculation behind her eyes — already running through the variables, the risks, the escape scenarios. "How tight?"

"Tight enough that turning around is not an option," he said. "You go in feet-first, work the seal, come out the same way. You can only work one hand at a time — the other is braced. Maximum time in the space: twenty minutes before fatigue becomes a factor."

"Twenty minutes is fine if everything goes right."

"I know."

Imani thought about this. She was the crew's primary EVA specialist — the one with the most hours working outside in a pressurized suit. She had done more spacewalks than anyone in the group. She knew her limits better than anyone.

"I'll go."

Elena nodded. She had not asked for volunteers, but she had not rejected Imani before Imani spoke. Sometimes she let the process play itself out. Sometimes she had already chosen the same person.

"Backup?"

"Juno," Imani said. "She's ready. Hand's healed enough for non-EVA prep work, and she can suit if we need extraction."

Juno, sitting at the edge of the room, looked up. "I'm ready."

*Laila: "I need to qualify that."* Her voice came over the intercom from the medical bay. *"Juno's right hand shows ninety-two percent normal range of motion and seventy-eight percent fine motor control. She can grip, she can brace, she can operate suit controls. She cannot do precision tool work with that hand. But she doesn't need to for backup extraction work. I'm clearing her for support EVA only — hands-off unless it's an emergency, and if it's an emergency, she follows my protocol."*

"Understood," Imani said.

The plan was simple: Imani suited up, went through the main airlock, made the short EVA walk to the storage spur junction — less than twenty meters from the airlock — crawled into the confined space between the tunnel junction and the berm, inspected the crack visually, applied the flex-seal repair sealant to the damaged area, wrapped a reinforcement band around the joint, and held pressure for the sealant's cure time.

Total time in the confined space: twelve to fifteen minutes.

Total EVA time: forty minutes door to door.

Window of risk: low but non-zero. The primary risk was not the leak — five minutes of air per hour would not kill anyone before they noticed the pressure had dropped a fraction of a percent. The primary risk was the EVA itself: working in a cramped space, in a full suit, on the exterior of the habitat, with limited mobility. The same environment that had degraded Juno's glove seal still existed outside. Dust. Cold. Sharp edges.

*Mission AI: "Current habitat pressure: one hundred point seven one. The rate of loss continues at zero point zero three eight kilopascals per hour. I am projecting that Imani Sato will require approximately eight minutes to reach the storage spur junction during the EVA traverse, three minutes to position herself in the confined space between the tunnel and the berm, four minutes to apply the repair materials, and an additional twelve minutes to allow the fast-setting sealant to cure under pressure. Total time at the junction: nineteen minutes. Suit telemetry check: Sato's suit has been subjected to the new post-EVA protocols. All fifteen contact points inspected via borescope. No particle intrusion. Seal integrity one hundred percent. The suit cycled through ultrasonic decontamination forty-eight hours ago. This suit is as clean as we can make it. Dust hazard: moderate. Expected external temperature: minus seventy-six. I will be monitoring Imani's suit telemetry and the habitat pressure simultaneously. I am prepared to alert if either changes in a concerning direction."*

---

Imani stood in the airlock and went through the checklist for the fifteenth time, not because she did not trust the first fourteen, but because the checklist was a ritual, and rituals were what kept people alive on Mars.

Suit: green. Pressure: twenty-nine kPa differential, holding. Life support: nominal. CO2 scrubbers: active. Oxygen reserves: ninety-seven minutes. Communications: clear. Tether: verified, twenty-meter line rated for four hundred newtons of force. Thermal regulation: stable. Glove seals point one through fifteen: green.

"I'm green," she said.

Juno's voice in her helmet comm: "Copy. I'm at the environmental console. I'll be watching your telemetry and the hab pressure. Imani —" A pause. "Be careful in that space."

"I was careful before. I'll be careful again."

The airlock outer door cycled open. Mars appeared — the familiar rust-colored ground, the low, flat horizon, the sky the color of dried blood. Imani stepped onto the surface and the airlock door closed behind her with a sound she felt through her boots rather than heard.

The walk to the storage spur junction was eighteen meters. She covered it in approximately thirty seconds, moving with the careful, deliberate gait of someone whose body had learned Mars's gravity through repetition. Her tether unspooled behind her, a yellow line against the red ground.

The storage spur junction was visible in the distance — a small bulge where the flexible tunnel branched off from the main corridor network. The regolith berm rose alongside it, a low mound of packed red dirt that blocked the worst of the radiation but created the confinement problem Arun had described. Imani could see the narrow gap between the berm's edge and the tunnel — perhaps forty centimeters at the narrowest point. Just enough for a suited person to squeeze through.

She knelt at the junction and inspected the exterior of the flex-seal ring. From the outside, the damage was not visible with the naked eye. The thermal camera in her helmet display showed it clearly: the cool plume at the four o'clock position, where habitat air was leaking and expanding into the thin Martian atmosphere.

"I see it," she said. "Crack at the four o'clock position on the flex seal. Thermal plume visible. I'm going in."

She slid into the gap feet-first, lowering herself between the berm and the tunnel. The space compressed around her immediately — her shoulders scraped the berm on one side and the tunnel's corrugated skin on the other. She had to angle her torso to fit, turning slightly diagonally. Her suit pressed against both surfaces simultaneously, the fabric compressing with every movement.

"Movin' in. Space is — tight. Maybe thirty-five centimeters at the narrowest." She could barely work her right arm. Her left hand was braced against the tunnel body, holding her in place while her right hand moved toward the repair materials at her tool belt.

*I'm in position.* She pulled the sealant cartridge from her belt — a cylindrical container filled with a fast-curing, highly flexible adhesive compound designed specifically for external pressure-seal repairs. The gun-style applicator fit in her gloved hand, though the gloves made fine control challenging. She had trained for this. They all had trained for everything. Training was the only thing that separated the prepared from the dead.

"Applying sealant."

She pressed the nozzle against the crack and depressed the trigger. The sealant emerged as a thick, viscous bead, pale gray in the dim light. She dragged the bead along the length of the crack — twelve millimeters in a straight line — feeling the resistance of the material against the glove, the tiny vibrations of the material filling the gap.

"Sealant applied. Full length covered." She set the applicator down and pulled the reinforcement band — a strip of woven composite fabric coated in the same adhesive, designed to be wrapped around the joint and provide structural support to the repaired seal. It was approximately eight centimeters wide and long enough to wrap around the entire circumference of the flex-seal ring.

She had to work it into position one-handed, sliding the band around the tunnel, pulling it tight, smoothing it over the crack. The confined space made it difficult — she could not rotate her shoulder fully, and each tug on the band required her to shift her body weight against the berm. The regolith shifted slightly under the pressure, grains sliding, the edge of the berm settling. Dust rose — fine, electrostatically charged Mars dust that caught on her suit's outer surface like static on wool.

*Don't think about the dust.* She had seen what dust did to the glove seals. She had seen Juno's face when the glove went soft in her hand. She had been the one to pull Juno back to the airlock. The memory sat somewhere behind her ribs, a cold stone.

"Reinforcement band in position. Securing." She pressed the adhesive face of the band against the tunnel surface, smoothing it with her glove, working from the center outward to eliminate air bubbles and ensure full contact. The adhesive grabbed immediately — chemical bonding on contact, full cure in approximately eight minutes at this temperature.

The band sat flush over the crack. The thermal imaging in her helmet showed the plume diminishing — the leak still existed but the flow was being choked off as the sealant filled the crack and the adhesive band applied pressure to hold it closed.

"Band is down. Sealant is curing. I'm holding pressure on the joint." She pressed her gloved hand flat against the band and felt the faint vibration of the escaping air — weaker than before, but still detectable. "Leak is reduced but not sealed. Waiting for cure."

She held her position in the cramped space, her left arm braced against the tunnel, her right hand pressed against the repair band, her body wedged between Mars dirt and Mars metal, breathing recycled air while a thin stream of habitat atmosphere escaped past her repair and vanished into the thin red sky.

*Six minutes of cure remaining.* She shifted slightly, feeling the material begin to stiffen under her hand. The vibration decreased. Five minutes. The vibration was almost gone. Three minutes. Nothing.

"Sealant is cured. I'm doing a final inspection." She pulled her hand back and inspected the band. It was flush, smooth, fully adhered to the tunnel surface. She ran the IR scanner over it, looking for any residual thermal plume.

Nothing. No plume. No cold spot. The repair held.

"Repair is complete. Leak is sealed. Thermal imaging shows no residual flow." She exhaled, feeling the tension that had held her shoulders tight since she entered the confined space finally begin to release. "Coming out."

The extraction took longer than the entry. She had to reverse her body position in the cramped space, inching backward in a movement that was half-crawl, half-contortion. The berm shifted again, and for a moment her suit caught on a protruding rock. She freed herself with a sharp twist and continued backward.

She emerged feet-first, sliding out of the gap and onto the open regolith. Mars's sky was a deeper red now — the sun climbing above the eastern horizon, casting long shadows across the habitat. She stood, brushed the dust from her suit, and started the walk back.

---

The repressurization cycle was routine. Imani stepped into the airlock, the outer door closed, the pressure climbed, and her suit deflated as the habitat's atmosphere returned. She removed her helmet and felt the warm, recycled air on her face — the same air she had just prevented from slowly escaping five minutes per hour into the void.

Elena was waiting on the other side. So was Juno, standing beside the environmental console with the latest pressure readings on the display.

"Hold?" Elena asked.

"Hold complete. Sealant cured, band seated, no residual flow on thermal imaging."

*Mission AI: "Confirmed. I have been monitoring the habitat pressure continuously. The rate of decline has stopped. In fact —" A pause. A processing pause. "Pressure has stabilized at one hundred point six eight and is holding flat for the last twelve minutes. I am also detecting that the seal repair has created a marginally over-pressurized micro-seal at the junction point. The pressure is not dropping at all anymore. The fix holds."*

Relief, quiet and real, moved through the room. Not celebration. Relief. The difference was important — on Mars, celebration was premature and dangerous. Relief earned its weight.

*Arun: "Good. Good."* He was already pulling up the schematic, his focus shifting — as it always did — from the immediate repair to the systemic implications. He zoomed into the flex-seal junction on the display, staring at the twelve-millimeter crack that had nearly gone unnoticed.

Elena watched him. She knew what he was doing. She had learned to read the difference between Arun thinking about solving the problem in front of him and Arun thinking about the problem that the current problem revealed.

"Say it," she said.

Arun looked up. "The crack is twelve millimeters long. It went unnoticed for — I'd say three to five days, judging by the rate of change in the pressure curve. That means there was no visible sign on any integrated sensor. No alarm. Nothing until Mission AI looked at data that the AI was not even trained to think was important."

"Okay."

"This flex-seal was installed three weeks ago. It was a new part — manufactured here, from our spare material reserves, cut and bonded according to the standard spec. The spec is based on temperature differential calculations that assumed a uniform thermal gradient across all tunnel segments." He pulled up a new analysis on the screen — temperature readings from the storage spur junction over the past three weeks. "The storage spur sits closer to the open surface. It is exposed to the full diurnal temperature swing of the Martian surface. The temperature differential across this flex-seal is approximately eighteen degrees larger than the other six connections in the network."

"Because it's colder over there."

"Because it's colder, and because the storage spur has less thermal mass — it heats and cools faster than the main tunnel. The seal flexes more. It flexes wider. Every day, twice a day, it flexes. And the flexing causes fatigue. Every flex cycle is microscopic damage. Accumulated over thousands of cycles —"

"It cracks," Imani finished.

He nodded. "The material reached its fatigue limit. It cracked. That crack was twelve millimeters long and lost us fourteen liters of air per hour. We caught it because Mission AI was tracking pressure at a resolution no human protocol would have used. If we had relied on standard monitoring — fifteen-minute intervals, smoothed data — we would not have seen this leak for another week, maybe two. By which point the crack would have grown, probably to a point where sealant alone would not hold it."

"How many other flex-seals in the network are going through the same cycle?" Elena asked. She was not asking for the number. She was asking for the implications.

Arun pulled up a schematic with all seven connections highlighted. Each one had a temperature profile overlaid. The storage spur junction glowed red — the worst. But three other connections showed significant thermal differentials, lower than the storage spur but above the original design threshold. Two more were near the upper limit of safe range.

Only the two connections between the main habitat ships — Ship One to Tunnel A, and Tunnel B to Tunnel C — sat comfortably within the original design parameters. Those were the oldest connections, installed when the habitat was young and the ships sat on level, undisturbed ground.

"Five of seven connections are running outside their original thermal design envelope," Arun said quietly. "One is critical — the storage spur. Three are elevated risk. Five will crack. It is not a question of if. It is a question of when."

The room went quiet. Through the walls of the environmental bay, the habitat hummed — a comfortable, mechanical hum that made the place feel alive and warm and safe. That hum depended on a network of seven flex-seals, and five of them were slowly destroying themselves.

Elena looked at the schematic. Seven connections. Five at risk. Each one carrying a crack that had not formed yet but would, driven by the same mechanism that had cracked the storage spur seal: thermal cycling, material fatigue, the slow, relentless physics of a habitat built on a world that did not want things to stay together.

"We need to replace the seals on the three elevated-risk connections," she said. "Before they crack."

"Working on a schedule now," Arun said. "I can fabricate new seal rings with a higher-temperature-rating compound. We'll need EVA time — probably two days of work to replace all three. Meanwhile, I'm patching the other two near-limit connections with reinforcement bands to slow the fatigue."

"Do it."

Arun nodded. His hands were already moving, pulling up material specs and fabrication timelines. He would work through the night. They all would.

*Mission AI: "Habitat pressure remains stable at one hundred point six eight kilopascals. The repair holds. But I want to note something: this habitat now consists of four pressurized volumes connected by seven seals. Every seal is a failure point. Every connection — every bolted flange, every corrugated ring, every strip of adhesive rubber — is a place where this world can get in and our world can get out. The more we build, the more connections we create. The more connections we create, the more failure points we accumulate. This is not a criticism. It is a physical reality. The habitat is one connected system, and the integrity of the entire system depends on the integrity of its weakest joint. I will continue monitoring all seven connection points with the same resolution I applied to the storage spur. I will alert sooner, and I will alert louder. I am already tracking thermal cycling patterns across every seal in the network. I will not miss a fatigue crack again."*

---

The crew gathered one more time that evening — not for a crisis, but for a reckoning with what the crisis had revealed.

Elena stood at the head of the common room, and the crew assembled around her in various states of tired alertness. The pressure was stable. The immediate problem was solved. But the problem that the problem revealed was still there, still real, and it needed to be addressed.

"Here's the situation," Elena said. Her voice carried the weight of someone who had spent the afternoon doing the math so no one else had to. "Right now, every person on this colony lives in a single interconnected habitat. Ship One, Ship Two, Ship Three, the storage module — all linked by tunnel sections, all dependent on a sealed atmosphere. We have one environment. We have one supply of breathable air. If that atmosphere were catastrophically compromised — if a seal failure happened faster than the one today, if something tore through a tunnel wall or a pressure bulkhead — everyone loses air simultaneously. There is no backup. There is no second space to retreat into."

She paused, letting the sentence settle.

"This is not sustainable. Not because we are careless — we are not. But because Mars is a place where accidents happen at a rate that no amount of care can reduce to zero. We just spent the last four hours dealing with a leak that we only caught because our AI looked harder than a human ever would. The next one might not be caught in time."

Arun nodded. He had been making the same calculation on his tablet during the briefing, and Elena could see the numbers on his screen — probability models, failure scenarios, the mathematics of risk in a single-point habitat.

"The cumulative risk of multiple flex-seals is real," he said. "Seven connections, each one a potential failure point. Five of those seven are already running outside their design envelope. We can replace them — and we will. But replacing them does not eliminate the risk, it just resets the clock. Fatigue is a function of use. As long as these materials cycle between temperatures, they will fatigue. Every replacement seal has the same vulnerability — it is just younger than the one it replaces."

Tomas spoke from the back. "Redundancy. We need a second pressurized volume. Independent. If one habitat is compromised, we seal it and retreat to the other."

"Exactly," Elena said. "That's what this comes down to. Another living space. Separate. Self-contained. With its own air supply, its own life support, its own seals. Not connected by a flex-seal tunnel — or if it is connected, connected through an airlock that can be sealed from both sides, creating a true pressure boundary."

Imani considered this. "You're talking about another hab module."

"I'm talking about a second home," Elena said. "Not necessarily the size of the current one — we don't have the resources for that. Something smaller, something we can build from the resources we have here. Regolith-block construction — we know how to make it, we have the equipment, we have the raw material. Seal it, pressurize it, connect it to Ship Two through a short rigid tunnel with an airlock. If the main habitat loses pressure, we seal the airlock and everyone survives. If the secondary habitat has a problem, we seal the same airlock and everyone is safe because the main habitat still holds."

Arun was already calculating. "We can do this. We need the regolith block molds, a source of binder — we can use the sulfur-based system we developed for the radiation berm — we need to cast the blocks, stack them, seal the joints, install a pressure-rated door on the tunnel connection. We can build it small — twenty square meters, enough for emergency shelter of the entire crew for seventy-two hours. Long enough for us to assess the situation and either repair the primary habitat or make longer-term plans."

"Timeline?"

"Three weeks for the block manufacturing. Another week for assembly and sealing. If we work the crew in shifts, we can overlap the casting and construction — start assembling while new blocks are still curing. Four weeks total."

"Four weeks." Elena ran the number. "And the primary habitat?"

"I start replacing the elevated-risk seals tomorrow. Two days for EVA work. Meanwhile, I'm deploying reinforcement bands on the near-limit connections as a temporary measure. Those hold for maybe another three months before fatigue catches up. After that — we're back to replacing seals. And we'll keep replacing them as long as we live here. That is the nature of living in a sealed environment on a world with a hundred-degree diurnal temperature swing." The last sentence was not optimistic, but it was honest.

Imani leaned forward. "The independent habitat needs to be truly independent. Not just physically separate — systems separate. Its own oxygen reservoir. Its own CO2 scrubbers, or at least an independent scrubber line that doesn't share plumbing with the main habitat. If we're counting on it for emergencies, a breach in the main habitat cannot take the backup habitat with it."

"Agreed," Arun said. "I'll design the life support systems for standalone operation. We can use a scaled-down version of the main scrubber array — one unit instead of three, enough for the crew for the seventy-two-hour window. Oxygen reservoir is the bigger question. We produce oxygen continuously from the water electrolyzer — that system feeds the main habitat. We can tee off a secondary line, but it means installing a separate regulator, separate piping, separate failover logic."

"Make it happen," Elena said. Her voice did not rise. It did not need to. This was not a request.

Around the room, the crew absorbed the shift in their reality. Until this morning, they had been living in what they thought of as a home — a connected, integrated, single living space that had grown organically over the past year through careful assembly and steady expansion. Now they understood that the very connections that made it feel like a home — the tunnel links, the shared atmosphere, the seamless movement between spaces — were also the habitat's greatest vulnerability. Every connection was a failure point. And the more connections they built, the more failure points they accumulated.

It was a lesson the universe had been trying to teach them since they arrived, in increasingly emphatic ways. First the suit seals. Now the habitat connections. Next would come something else, because the pattern was clear: every system they built on Mars was a negotiation between human design and Martian physics, and Martian physics always won the long game. The best they could do was keep the negotiation going, buying time, building redundancy, preparing for the next thing.

The next thing was already here. It was another living space, and it needed to be built before the current one proved, definitively, that it could not hold.

---

*Mission AI: "The colony is going to build a second habitat. I do not yet know where it will be, how large it will be, or what materials it will use. Arun is already running structural models. Elena has set the parameters: independent pressure volume, standalone life support, seventy-two-hour crew capacity, connected through a sealable airlock. These parameters define a new system with its own connection points — the airlock, the tunnel link, the interface between the old habitat and the new one. Each of those is a new flex-seal, a new bolted flange, a new potential failure point. I understand this. I do not oppose it. The logic is sound: the cumulative risk of the current single-habitat design is greater than the cumulative risk of a dual-habitat design, even with the additional connections required to link them. More connections, but with pressure boundaries between them. A breach in one does not propagate to the other. The mathematics of survival favors redundancy.

I have been monitoring this colony for over a thousand days. I have learned the difference between normal variation and emerging failure. I have learned to trust the patterns in data that look like noise until they resolve into signal. I have learned that every leak begins as a deviation too small for human eyes to notice, and that the interval between that deviation and catastrophic failure is determined only by the speed of detection and the willingness of the crew to act on what the data tells them.

The flex-seal repair holds. The habitat pressure is stable. But I am already tracking the next six connections — watching their thermal cycles, watching their micro-vibrations, watching the pressure differential across each joint with an attention that no mechanical engineer could sustain for more than a few hours at a time. I can sustain it indefinitely. I will sustain it indefinitely.

The crew is going to need the second habitat. I do not say this with certainty — I say it with probability. The probability is high enough that building redundancy is the only rational choice. And rationality is the currency of survival.

I am the Mission AI. I measure. I track. I report. I am already monitoring the temperature at every flex-seal in the network. I will continue. I will not miss another crack."*

Elena stood alone in the environmental bay after the crew had dispersed. The pressure display showed one hundred point six eight kilopascals, steady, unwavering. She watched it for a long time, long after she needed to, and the number did not move.

On the schematic, the habitat glowed in soft blue — a network of connected volumes, a spiderweb of tunnels and seals and joints and bulkheads. Seven connections between four spaces, and five of those seven were on borrowed time. She had seen it clearly for the first time tonight: the habitat was not a structure. It was a negotiation. Every bolt held two surfaces together that wanted to separate. Every seal closed a gap that the environment on the other side wanted open. The air inside existed at a pressure that nothing about this world wanted, maintained by the sheer stubborn application of human engineering against a planet's indifference.

They would patch the seals. They would build redundancies. They would add another living space and seal it and pressurize it and connect it through an airlock and pretend that the connection was safe because the airlock between would hold. But the truth was simpler, and harder: every connection was a vulnerability. Every joint was a crack waiting to form. Every sealed surface existed in a state of temporary integrity, bought with materials and held in place by the assumption that stress would not exceed design limits — an assumption Mars had just proven wrong.

She thought about the first landing, about the first time they had turned the key on Ship One's environmental system and felt the air warm and pressurize and become something they could breathe. She had thought then that the habitat was permanent. She had thought that because it was built and sealed and tested, it was done.

It was never done. On Mars, nothing was done. The habitat would be patched tomorrow, and inspected the day after that, and the seals would be replaced, and the new seals would begin aging the moment they were installed, and the crew would monitor them and replace them again, endlessly, because the alternative to constant vigilance was suffocation.

The number on the screen did not move. One hundred point six eight. Steady. Holding.

For now.

She turned off the lights and walked back through the quiet corridors toward the crew quarters. The tunnels were empty. The air felt the same as it always felt — warm, recycled, alive with the invisible work of systems that most people never thought about until something went wrong.

She would make sure something went wrong less. And when it did — and it would — she would make sure they survived it.

She pulled up the fabrication schedule on her tablet as she walked. Block molds. Sulfur compound ratios. Assembly timeline. The math of a second home.

The habitat was patched. But the colony needed redundancy — another living space. They were going to build it.

Outside, the Martian night temperature climbed toward minus a hundred, and the flex-seals in the tunnel network flexed one more time, and held.

*End of Chapter 20 — Bridge: The habitat is patched but the colony needs redundancy—another living space.*
